what_its_for: Trastuzumab-dttb is a cancer medicine used to treat certain types of breast cancer and stomach cancer that have a protein called HER2 on the surface of the cancer cells. Your doctor will test your cancer to make sure it is HER2-positive before starting this medicine. It works by attaching to the HER2 protein and helping your immune system fight and slow the growth of cancer cells.
how_to_take: This medicine is given as an intravenous (IV) infusion, meaning it goes directly into your vein through a needle or catheter. A nurse or healthcare provider will give you this medication in a clinic or hospital setting. You will NOT give this injection to yourself at home. Your first infusion is usually given slowly over about 90 minutes. If you tolerate it well, later infusions may be given over about 30 minutes. Stay at the clinic for observation after each infusion so staff can watch for any reactions.
dosing: Your doctor will calculate your dose based on your body weight in kilograms. The usual starting dose is 8 mg/kg given once as a loading dose, followed by maintenance doses of 6 mg/kg given every 3 weeks. Some regimens use a weekly dose of 4 mg/kg followed by 2 mg/kg weekly. Your doctor will decide the exact schedule that is right for you based on your specific cancer and treatment plan. Never change your dose or schedule without talking to your doctor first.
missed_dose: Because this medicine is given by a healthcare provider in a clinic, it is very important to keep all of your scheduled appointments. If you miss or need to reschedule an infusion, call your doctor or clinic right away to set up a new appointment as soon as possible. Do not try to double up on doses to make up for a missed one. Your doctor will guide you on the best next steps.
storage: You will not store this medicine at home since it is prepared and given in a healthcare facility. For your awareness: the pharmacy stores the unmixed powder in a refrigerator at 36°F to 46°F (2°C to 8°C). Once it is mixed and ready to use, it must be used promptly or stored in the refrigerator and used within 24 hours. Never freeze the mixed solution.
what_to_avoid: Tell your doctor or pharmacist about ALL medicines, vitamins, supplements, and herbal products you take before starting this medicine. Avoid becoming pregnant while on this medicine, as it can harm an unborn baby. Use effective birth control during treatment and for 7 months after your last dose. Do not breastfeed during treatment and for 7 months after your last dose. Avoid activities that require full alertness if you feel dizzy or tired after infusions. Limit alcohol and smoking as they can affect your overall health and cancer recovery.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or get emergency help RIGHT AWAY if you have: chest pain, shortness of breath, or trouble breathing; severe cough; swelling of your ankles or legs; rapid weight gain; feeling faint or very dizzy; fast or irregular heartbeat; fever, chills, shaking, or nausea during or after your infusion; rash, itching, hives, or swelling of your face, lips, or throat; severe headache or confusion; any signs of infection such as fever above 100.4°F, unusual bruising or bleeding; or if you think you may be pregnant. These could be signs of serious side effects that need immediate medical attention.
when_it_works: This medicine starts working right away on a cellular level, but you may not feel changes immediately. Most people begin to see benefits after several weeks to months of treatment. Your doctor will monitor your progress through regular check-ups, lab tests, and imaging scans. Heart function tests (like an echocardiogram or MUGA scan) will also be checked regularly because this medicine can affect your heart. Treatment may continue for many months or as long as it is helping and you are tolerating it well. Always keep your follow-up appointments so your doctor can track how well the medicine is working.
special_populations: Pregnancy: This medicine can cause serious harm or death to an unborn baby, especially if used in the second or third trimester. Tell your doctor immediately if you become pregnant. Use effective birth control during treatment and for 7 months after stopping. Breastfeeding: Do not breastfeed during treatment or for 7 months after your last dose. Heart problems: This medicine can weaken the heart muscle. Tell your doctor if you have a history of heart disease, high blood pressure, or have received certain other cancer medicines (like anthracyclines such as doxorubicin). Your heart will be monitored regularly. Elderly patients: Older adults may be more sensitive to side effects, especially heart-related effects. Kidney or liver problems: Dose adjustments are generally not required, but inform your doctor of any kidney or liver issues. Children: This medicine is not approved for use in children.
